title: The heroes of faith (Hebrews 11:17–40)
hook: Moses, Rahab, Gideon, and unnamed ones of whom the world was not worthy
tomorrow: what do you say to someone whose knees have given up?

segments.voice: Abraham packed light, went out not knowing whither, and lived in tents. Faith: the evidence of things not seen. The list keeps going, and it gets crowded.
screen: `THE EVIDENCE OF THINGS NOT SEEN.` → `THE LIST GETS CROWDED.`

segments.voice: At the end of a movie, the credits roll past the stars and keep going: the driver, the caterer, the person who held the light. Most people are already walking out. Hebrews eleven has credits like that. Halfway down its list, the writer runs short of time: "And what shall I more say? for the time would fail me to tell of Gedeon, and of Barak, and of Samson, and of Jephthae; of David also, and Samuel, and of the prophets." The names come faster and faster. And then they stop, and a plainer word takes over: others.
screen: `THE CREDITS NOBODY READS.` → `THE TIME WOULD FAIL ME.` → `THEN: OTHERS.`

segments.voice: The named ones first. Moses "refused to be called the son of Pharaoh's daughter." Rahab of Jericho "received the spies with peace." Some on this list won. They "stopped the mouths of lions," and "out of weakness were made strong." But others didn't win. They were mocked, chained, driven out, and "wandered about in sheepskins and goatskins." No names at all. And right there, mid-sentence, the writer stops to add: "Of whom the world was not worthy." The world counted them as nobody. Hebrews turns it around: the world wasn't good enough for them. Then a twist: "And these all, having obtained a good report through faith, received not the promise." Not even the famous ones. God, the writer says, had something better in view, "that they without us should not be made perfect." Nobody crosses the line alone. So what does this give you for an ordinary week? A new way to read the room. The person refilling the coffee, the aide on the night shift, the neighbor who always shows up: Hebrews puts people like that in the same chapter as Moses, and gives them its highest line.
screen: `MOSES, RAHAB: THE NAMED ONES.` · `SOME WON; OTHERS DIDN'T.` · `OF WHOM THE WORLD WAS NOT WORTHY.` · `NOBODY CROSSES ALONE.` · then, large: `THE WORLD WAS NOT WORTHY.`

segments.voice: Count three people whose work you leaned on today without knowing their names: who stocked the shelf, drove the bus, cleaned the hallway, answered the phone. Give each one a slow breath and a silent thank you, the way Hebrews gives the unnamed a line of their own.
The heroes of faith. The crowded end of Hebrews eleven: Moses and Rahab, and the others whose names nobody kept.
Pocket this one: the world was not worthy, said of people with no names in the story. Peace to you.

howItsDone: Christians remember the faithful of Hebrews 11 in sermons and study, and some churches also keep days to remember saints and believers whose names are not known.

fork.setup: at your great-aunt's funeral, the program thanks the pastor, the soloist, the pallbearers. nobody mentions the neighbor who drove her to every appointment. what does Hebrews 11 do with people like that?
options: leaves them out; lists are for the famous.
says they'll get their names in a later list.
gives them its highest line: the world was not worthy.
fork.reveal: Hebrews runs out of names and keeps going: others, of whom the world was not worthy. the unnamed get the chapter's most honoring words.

original.note: Greek: worthy. Hebrews 11:38, of whom the world was not worthy.

trapdoor: what you thought: heroes of faith means the winners.
what it means: the list holds winners and losers, named and unnamed, and gives the nameless ones its highest line.
what a scholar hears: these all received not the promise; Hebrews keeps even the famous waiting, that they without us should not be made perfect.

recall: gather to stir one another to love

chat.says: night aide at rehab hums hymns to pop at 3am. nobody knows her last name. how do i thank her?
options: Ask her name and tell her what it meant. Hebrews says of the unnamed: the world was not worthy.
Don't bother. Hebrews 11 only remembers the famous ones, like Moses and David, who won.
Just thank God. Hebrews says the unnamed ones never wanted anyone on earth to notice.
chat.meaning: Hebrews 11 runs out of names and honors the others anyway: of whom the world was not worthy. Faithful, unnoticed people deserve to be named.

Gedeon.meaning: the King James spelling of Gideon, a judge of Israel

Jephthae.meaning: the King James spelling of Jephthah, a judge of Israel

Rahab.meaning: a woman of Jericho who sheltered Israel's spies

notes: Written 2026-10-13 in the year-2-4 recipe; rewritten 2026-10-15 in recipe v3. Title, word, carry and sources kept. Isaac's binding (11:17–19) was cut from the voice for length.

For parents: 'mocked, chained, driven out' paraphrases Hebrews 11:36–37 (cruel mockings, bonds and imprisonment, stoned, sawn asunder, slain with the sword); the harder details are left out on purpose.

'Something better in view' paraphrases 11:40 ('some better thing for us'). 'Its highest line' is the writer's description of 'of whom the world was not worthy', not a claim the text makes; confirm the tone.
The index hook names Gideon; the lesson uses the KJV spelling Gedeon inside the quotation and glosses it.
howItsDone: 'some churches also keep days to remember saints and believers whose names are not known' (e.g. All Saints) is a general practice claim; confirm.
v3 life shape: an ordinary week (the people who keep things going unnoticed) and what the passage gives for it.
